Window
WIN-dō
n. (rendering Hebrew challōn and 'arūbbâh, and Greek thuris)
From Old Norse vindauga, literally wind-eye — the opening through which the wind comes and through which the house sees. The compound is one of the most vivid survivals in English, and it happens to match the Hebrew usage closely, since 'arūbbâh means a lattice or sluice and is the word for the windows of heaven, openings through which what is above is poured down upon what is below.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The window in Scripture is an opening in a barrier, and its theology follows from that: it is the point at which what is outside comes in, or what is inside is let out. Heaven has windows, and they are opened for judgment and for blessing alike. At the flood “the windows of heaven were opened” (Gen 7:11), and the same phrase in Malachi becomes the great promise attached to the tithe: “prove me now herewith…if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it” (Mal 3:10). The window is also the way of escape for those under the protection of a promise. Rahab “let them down by a cord through the window” (Jos 2:15), and the scarlet line she was to bind in that same window became the mark that saved her house — a window that is at once the means of deliverance for the spies and the sign of deliverance for her family. Paul was let down by the wall in a basket through a window at Damascus. And a window can be the place of judgment: Jezebel looked out at a window and was cast down; Michal looked through a window and despised David in her heart; Eutychus “sat in a window…being fallen into a deep sleep” and fell to his death and was raised (Act 20:9). Daniel's windows are the most deliberate of all: knowing the writing was signed, he went into his house, his windows being open toward Jerusalem, and prayed as he did aforetime — open windows as a refusal to hide obedience.

Webster 1828 Definition

An opening in a wall to admit light and air; in Scripture the aperture of heaven opened for flood or for blessing, the means of escape for Rahab's spies and for Paul, and the place of both judgment and open, unhidden prayer.

expand to see more

WINDOW, n. 1. An opening in the wall of a building for the admission of light, and of air when necessary.

2. The word is from wind and eye, the Danish vindue, an opening through which the wind passes and the house looks out.

3. In Scripture, the windows of heaven; the openings through which rain is poured, used both of the flood and of abundant blessing. Gen. 7; Mal. 3.

4. A lattice; the ancient windows were closed with lattice work rather than with glass. Through the window she looked, and cried through the lattice. Judges 5.

5. Daniel's windows being open toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day; a testimony of prayer not concealed from adversaries. Dan. 6.

Key Scripture

Genesis 7:11 — "In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, the seventeenth day of the month, the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened."

Joshua 2:15 — "Then she let them down by a cord through the window: for her house was upon the town wall, and she dwelt upon the wall."

Malachi 3:10 — "Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it."

Acts 20:9 — "And there sat in a window a certain young man named Eutychus, being fallen into a deep sleep: and as Paul was long preaching, he sunk down with sleep, and fell down from the third loft, and was taken up dead."

Modern Corruption

Mal 3:10 has been detached from its covenant setting and turned into a formula of exchange, in which a payment triggers a guaranteed return of wealth — the one verse in Scripture where God says prove me, made into a lever.

expand to see more

The prosperity teaching rests more weight on this verse than on any other, and the misuse works by omission. Malachi is addressing a covenant nation under a covenant sanction: the whole nation was cursed with a curse because the whole nation had robbed God in tithes and offerings, and the storehouse is the temple storehouse that fed the Levites who had no inheritance. The promise of opened windows is the reversal of a national agricultural curse — the devourer rebuked, the vine not casting her fruit before the time. To lift it out and offer it to an individual as a guaranteed return on a donation is to promise what the text does not promise, and it consistently enriches the one collecting rather than the one giving.

What the passage does teach is worth keeping. God submits Himself to a test on the point of His people's giving, which He does nowhere else; He treats withheld offerings as robbery, which is a far graver category than stinginess; and the blessing He names is abundance beyond room to receive it. New Testament giving is not less than this but freer — every man according as he purposeth in his heart, not grudgingly or of necessity, for God loveth a cheerful giver — and it comes with the same assurance that God is able to make all grace abound. The difference is that the promise is of sufficiency for every good work, not of personal wealth on demand.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew challōn is the ordinary window of a house; 'arūbbâh is the lattice or sluice, the word in windows of heaven. Greek thuris, a diminutive of thura (door), is the New Testament term.

expand to see more

Hebrew challōn (H2474) — a window; the window of the ark, Rahab's window, Michal's window, and the window Jezebel looked out of.

Hebrew 'arūbbâh (H699) — a lattice, a sluice, a chimney; the word in the windows of heaven (Gen 7:11; Mal 3:10) and in the doves flying to their windows (Isa 60:8).

Hebrew eshnāb (H822) — a latticed window; used of Sisera's mother crying through the lattice (Jdg 5:28) and of the simple ones seen in Pro 7:6.

Greek thuris (G2376) — a window, little door; used only twice, of Paul let down through a window in a basket (2Co 11:33) and of Eutychus in the window at Troas.

Hebrew tsohar (H6672) — a light, an opening; the window commanded for the ark in Gen 6:16, a word otherwise meaning noon or brightness.

Usage

"Of the openings of heaven: the windows of heaven were opened (Gen 7:11); open you the windows of heaven (Mal 3:10); the LORD make windows in heaven (2Ki 7:2)."

"Of escape and deliverance: Rahab let them down by a cord through the window (Jos 2:15); Paul let down by the wall in a basket (Act 9:25)."

"Of what is seen or shewn through an opening: Michal looking through a window and despising David (2Sa 6:16); Daniel's windows open toward Jerusalem (Dan 6:10)."
